query: Which material can be used for enhanced catalytic activity and durability toward HER and HOR, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing interstitial dopants (oxygen or nitrogen) into a TaNbHfZrTi-based high-entropy alloy will enhance its catalytic activity and durability toward both HER and HOR by forming ordered interstitial complexes that serve as stable, active sites for hydrogen adsorption while also strengthening the alloy structurally under reaction conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi-based high-entropy alloy in its as-cast, minimally doped form.
generation.intervention: Interstitial doping with controlled amounts of oxygen or nitrogen to induce formation of ordered interstitial complexes within the alloy lattice.
generation.conditions: Electrochemical testing under typical HER/HOR conditions (e.g., in acidic or alkaline electrolyte at ambient temperature with appropriate potential cycling) to simulate practical operational environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ordered oxygen or nitrogen complexes (OOCs/ONCs) that modify the local atomic environment and create stable catalytic sites.
generation.mechanism: The ordered interstitial dopants are expected to facilitate hydrogen adsorption/desorption by modulating the local electronic structure, reducing activation barriers for HER and HOR. Simultaneously, these complexes enhance the mechanical and chemical durability of the alloy through solid-solution strengthening, ensuring stable performance under cycling conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The doped alloy will display lower overpotentials and faster kinetics (indicated by improved Tafel slopes) for HER and HOR, along with superior durability under prolonged electrochemical cycling compared to the undoped base HEA.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (overpotential, Tafel slope, durability under cycling) for the base Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA without interstitial doping.
generation.boundary: The direct link between the formation of ordered interstitial complexes in these HEAs and enhanced HER/HOR activity is not yet established; optimal dopant concentrations and their distribution may vary, and thus the precise magnitude of the effect is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: While the formation of ordered interstitial complexes is supported by evidence demonstrating improved damping and mechanical properties, there is insufficient direct evidence linking these complexes to enhanced catalytic HER/HOR activity. The hypothesis is thus contingent on the assumption that similar structural features beneficial for mechanical performance will also facilitate catalysis.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi-based HEA samples with varying levels of oxygen or nitrogen doping. Test the HER and HOR activity in a standard three-electrode electrochemical cell under controlled conditions (acidic/alkaline electrolyte, defined temperature, and applied potential cycling). Compare the overpotentials, Tafel slopes, and durability (performance retention over cycling) of the doped samples against an undoped control sample.
measurements: HER and HOR overpotential at a fixed current density
Stability/durability metrics (e.g., percentage retention of catalytic performance after a set number of cycles)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the interstitial-doped HEA does not exhibit at least a 10% reduction in overpotential and a measurable improvement in durability (e.g., slower performance degradation) compared to the undoped HEA, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
